implementation_notes: C has no authorization framework, so the classic Policy and Guard roles are written by hand: a policy struct holding the decision function (usually a table of function pointers or a rule array) plus a guard function that every protected operation calls before touching the resource. What replaces the classic structure: plain structs and function pointers replace the Policy/Guard class pair and virtual dispatch; the Linux kernel's security hooks, which core code invokes before an operation, are the system-scale instance of exactly this shape, and POSIX capabilities show how the OS models a subject's rights. The hand-written form is still justified where a check function genuinely is the enforcement point (embedded, kernel or protocol code); there is no lighter alternative that keeps rules out of resource code.
idiom_name: policy struct of function pointers + guard check function
pitfalls: With no namespaces or access control, one missing prototype in a shared header lets callers reach the resource without the guard; keep the policy/guard API and the resource accessors in one compilation unit or prefix.
A NULL or partially initialised subject is easy to pass in C and reads as 'no restriction' if the decision function only tests fields; deny on missing fields explicitly.
A global mutable rule table is not thread-safe; publish the policy read-only at start-up or protect it with the same lock discipline as the resource.
